deep.reconstruction:
Context: these are lecture-style notes, probably notes on practical astronomy, on the corrections of a meridian (transit) instrument. They continue the previous page. Notation: delta = declination, p = 90deg - delta = polar distance, phi = latitude, c = collimation error, i = inclination of the axis, a = azimuth error.

The previous page set out three forms of the transit-time correction:
- Tobias Mayer: tau = c/cos(delta) + i*cos(phi-delta)/cos(delta) + a*sin(phi-delta)/cos(delta).
- Hansen/Bessel: tau = m + n*tan(delta) + c*sec(delta). Expanding Mayer's form gives m = i*cos(phi) + a*sin(phi) and n = i*sin(phi) - a*cos(phi). The sign of the a-terms depends on the azimuth convention.
- Gauss: tau = m + C*cot(p/2) + I*tan(p/2). This uses sec(delta) = 1/sin p = (cot(p/2)+tan(p/2))/2 and tan(delta) = cot p = (cot(p/2)-tan(p/2))/2. Hence C = (c+n)/2, I = (c-n)/2 and C+I = c. The previous page writes C=(c-n)/2, which is an assignment or sign slip.

(1) Collimation (C) from Polaris at successive upper and lower culminations.
- At lower culmination the star crosses the meridian beyond the pole. In the formulas this is delta -> 180deg - delta, i.e. p -> -p, so sec(delta) and tan(delta) change sign. Equivalently cot(p/2) -> -cot(p/2) and tan(p/2) -> -tan(p/2).
- Upper-transit correction: m + C*cot(p/2) + I*tan(p/2). Lower-transit correction: m - C*cot(p/2) - I*tan(p/2).
- So, after allowing for the clock rate and the star's change of apparent place, the interval between the two transits differs from 12 sidereal hours by 2*C*cot(p/2) + 2*I*tan(p/2) = 2(c sec delta + n tan delta).
- For Polaris p is about 1.5deg. Then cot(p/2) is about 76 and tan(p/2) about 0.013, so the deviation is essentially 2*C*cot(p/2). This is what the page records (written as 2C cotg p/2; the I-term is dropped as negligible).

(2) The parenthesis expresses C through the setting-up (Aufstellung) errors m, n. It also inverts m, n back to the inclination: i = m*cos(phi) + n*sin(phi) with the convention above. The manuscript has 'm cos phi - n sin phi = i', which corresponds to the opposite sign convention for n/a.

(3) Alternative: observe upper and lower culmination of Polaris in both positions of the instrument (before and after reversal).
- Reversal changes c -> -c and leaves n unchanged. So C=(c+n)/2 -> (n-c)/2 = -I and I -> -C. This is the manuscript's 'C geht in -I über' (my reading).
- Position 1 gives D1 = 2C*cot(p/2) + 2I*tan(p/2). Position 2 gives D2 = -2I*cot(p/2) - 2C*tan(p/2).
- Solving these two linear equations gives C and I separately, hence c = C+I and n = C-I. This last step is mine, implicit in the text.

(4) Practical remark: when determining the setting-up errors one must check that the pivots are truly cylindrical. This is done by levelling (striding level) in different positions/inclinations of the telescope, i.e. the inequality-of-pivots test.
errors: Previous page: C=(c-n)/2 should be C=(c+n)/2 (with I=(c-n)/2) if C is the coefficient of cot(p/2) and the convention C+I=c is used. Possibly only a labeling slip.
The deviation from 12h is strictly 2C cot(p/2) + 2I tan(p/2). Writing only 2C cot(p/2) neglects the I-term, which is justified for Polaris (factor about 1/5800) but is an approximation.

The relation 'm cos phi - n sin phi = i' holds only with a particular sign convention for azimuth/n. With n = i sin phi - a cos phi the correct inversion is i = m cos phi + n sin phi. This is a sign-convention issue, not a substantive error.

results.what: Interval between upper and lower culmination of a circumpolar star differs from 12h by 2(c sec delta + n tan delta) = 2C cot(p/2) + 2I tan(p/2); for Polaris this gives the collimation-type constant C
results.modern_name: Determination of instrumental constants of a transit circle from upper/lower culminations of a close circumpolar star
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 19th-c. practical astronomy (Bessel, Gauss, Hansen; textbook in Brünnow, Chauvenet)

results.what: Gauss form m + C cot(p/2) + I tan(p/2) of the transit correction and the behaviour C -> -I under reversal of the instrument
results.modern_name: Gauss's half-polar-distance form of the transit-instrument reduction formula
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss (lectures/Göttingen practice), alongside Bessel/Hansen forms

results.what: Checking pivot cylindricity by levelling in different telescope positions
results.modern_name: Pivot inequality/irregularity test with the striding level

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine lecture notes on meridian-instrument corrections, probably notes on Gauss-school practical astronomy. Nothing goes beyond standard 19th-century textbook material.

checkable.asserts: Mayer form equals Hansen/Bessel m + n tan(delta) with m=i cos phi + a sin phi, n=i sin phi - a cos phi
Inversion i = m cos phi + n sin phi
Upper minus lower culmination correction (p -> -p) gives deviation 2C cot(p/2)+2I tan(p/2)
For p about 1.5deg, cot(p/2)/tan(p/2) is about 5800, justifying neglect of the I-term

transcription_corrections: '= 2 C [-cot g-] tg[?] p/2': cotg is the correct and intended function (deviation is about 2C cot(p/2)); the cancellation reading is doubtful.
'm cos^2[?] phi - n sin phi = c[?]' likely reads 'm cos phi - n sin phi = i' (the inclination expressed through m, n).
'Können[?] 3 Sterne[?] auf ... bestimmt werden' likely reads 'C und I können auch bestimmt werden'.
'also geht C in -C über' likely reads 'also geht C in -I über', which is mathematically correct since c->-c maps (c+n)/2 to -(c-n)/2.
